lead: An engine never burns all its fuel perfectly. Carbon monoxide (CO) comes from too little oxygen, unburnt hydrocarbons (HC) from fuel that the flame never reaches, and oxides of nitrogen (NOx) from a flame that is too hot. These are the three engine-out gases, measured before any catalytic converter. Each comes from a different failure, so one fix cannot remove all three, and every emission control that follows is built on these three routes.
prereq: You need: the stages of combustion and flame quenching (Combustion in SI and CI engines) and the idea of air–fuel ratio.

sections.h3: CO: the gas of a rich mixture

blocks.text: Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless, poisonous gas. It forms when carbon in the fuel is only partly oxidised: C + ½O<sub>2</sub> → CO. With enough oxygen, CO burns on to CO<sub>2</sub>, mainly through the reaction CO + OH → CO<sub>2</sub> + H.

blocks.where: φ is the equivalence ratio; F/A is the fuel–air ratio by mass. φ > 1 is rich, φ < 1 is lean. The air–fuel ratio is the inverse idea: for petrol the stoichiometric value is about 14.7, so φ = 0.9 means an air–fuel ratio of 14.7 ÷ 0.9 = 16.3. The excess air factor λ = 1/φ is used on oxygen sensors.

blocks.text: In a petrol engine CO depends almost only on φ. On the rich side there is not enough oxygen to finish the carbon, so CO climbs steeply: a few per cent by volume at φ = 1.2. At the high temperature of the burned gas some CO<sub>2</sub> also dissociates (CO<sub>2</sub> ⇌ CO + ½O<sub>2</sub>). During expansion the gas cools fast and the CO-burning reactions slow down and “freeze”, so even a stoichiometric or slightly lean engine leaves a small CO level, a few tenths of a per cent, above the low-temperature equilibrium value.
A diesel runs lean overall (φ about 0.3 to 0.8), so its engine-out CO is low. Some CO still comes from rich pockets in the spray and from lean regions too cool to finish burning.

sections.h3: Unburnt hydrocarbons: fuel that hides from the flame

blocks.text: Unburnt hydrocarbons are fuel molecules, and partly burnt pieces of them, that leave in the exhaust. An analyser counts them as carbon atoms, in ppm C1 (see the flame ionisation detector in emission measurement). In a petrol engine the main sources are:

items: Crevices: the narrow gap above the top piston ring (the top land), the ring grooves and the spark-plug thread. Mixture is pushed in during compression, the flame cannot enter a gap this narrow, and the mixture comes back out during expansion. Studies of petrol engines put crevices as the largest single source.
Oil film: fuel vapour dissolves in the oil on the liner while the pressure is high and comes out again after the flame has passed.
Wall quenching: the flame dies a short distance from a cold wall, typically about 0.1 mm. Most of this thin layer mixes with hot gas later and burns, so quenching adds less HC than crevices.
Liquid fuel and misfire: on a cold start fuel wets the port and the cylinder and evaporates too late; a cycle that misfires sends all its fuel out.
Valve overlap: when intake and exhaust valves are open together, a little fresh mixture can short-circuit to the exhaust.

blocks.text: Some of the HC that leaves the crevices and the oil film burns in the hot gas during expansion and in the exhaust port. That is why retarding the spark lowers HC: the exhaust leaves hotter, and more HC burns on the way out. It also lowers NOx, but costs fuel. HC falls as the mixture leans out, then rises again when the charge is so lean that flames die and cycles misfire. In a diesel, HC comes from over-lean edges of the spray and from fuel that dribbles out of the nozzle sac after injection ends.

sections.h3: NOx: the gas of a hot flame

blocks.text: NOx means nitric oxide (NO) plus nitrogen dioxide (NO2). In a petrol engine NO is almost all of it; in a diesel NO2 can be 10 to 30 per cent. Most NO is thermal NO, made from the nitrogen and oxygen of the air in the hot burned gas behind the flame.

Zeldovich mechanism: O + N2 → NO + N, then N + O2 → NO + O. Adding the third reaction N + OH → NO + H gives the extended Zeldovich mechanism. The first reaction must break the very strong N≡N bond, so it is slow below about 1800 K and speeds up sharply above it.

Thermal NO therefore needs three things together: high temperature, oxygen atoms, and time at that temperature. The peak sits slightly lean of stoichiometric, near φ = 0.9 (air–fuel ratio about 16): the burned gas is still very hot and some oxygen is left over. Richer, there is no spare oxygen; leaner, the extra air cools the flame. Anything that raises the peak burned gas temperature raises NO: advanced spark or injection, a higher compression ratio, high load and hot intake air. Exhaust gas recirculation, spark retard and charge cooling lower it. Small amounts also come from prompt NO in the flame front and from nitrogen bound in the fuel.

examples.question: A petrol engine passes 0.05 m³/s of dry exhaust, measured at standard conditions (0 °C, 1 atm), where the density of CO is 1.25 kg/m³. The NDIR analyser reads 0.4 % CO by volume and the brake power is 60 kW. Find the CO mass flow and the brake-specific CO in g/kWh.
steps: CO mass flow: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s × 1.25 kg/m³ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg/s = 0.25 g/s.
CO per hour: 0.25 g/s × 3600 s/h = 900 g/h.
Check the density: 28.0 kg/kmol ÷ 22.41 m³/kmol = 1.25 kg/m³ at 0 °C and 1 atm, so the data agree.
examples.answer: CO mass flow is 0.25 g/s and brake-specific CO is 15 g/kWh.

examples.question: A petrol engine burns 10 kg/h of fuel at φ = 0.9 (stoichiometric air–fuel ratio 14.7) and gives 40 kW. The analyser reads 2000 ppm NO in the wet exhaust, whose mean molar mass is 28.6 kg/kmol. Find the NOx in g/kWh. Emission rules count NOx as NO<sub>2</sub> (46.0 kg/kmol).
steps: Exhaust mass flow = air + fuel = 163.3 + 10 = 173.3 kg/h.
ppm is a mole fraction: NO flow = 2000 × 10⁻⁶ × 6.061 = 0.01212 kmol/h.
examples.answer: The engine emits about 558 g/h of NOx (as NO<sub>2</sub>), that is 13.9 g/kWh before any catalyst.

traps: Saying NOx is highest in the richest, hottest-sounding mixture. NO peaks slightly lean, near φ = 0.9, because it needs spare oxygen as well as heat.
Writing “φ = 0.9 means an air–fuel ratio of 15”. For petrol, φ = 0.9 is 14.7 ÷ 0.9 = 16.3.
Calling three reactions “the Zeldovich mechanism”. The first two are the Zeldovich (thermal) mechanism; with N + OH → NO + H it is the extended Zeldovich mechanism.
Naming wall quenching as the main HC source. Crevices are the largest; the quench layer is only about 0.1 mm and much of it burns later.
Converting ppm to mass with the molar mass of NO when the rule asks for NOx as NO<sub>2</sub>: the answer comes out 30/46 of the right value.

quiz.q: Define the equivalence ratio φ and give the air–fuel ratio of petrol at φ = 0.9.
quiz.a: φ = actual fuel–air ratio ÷ stoichiometric fuel–air ratio. At φ = 0.9 the air–fuel ratio is 14.7 ÷ 0.9 = 16.3.

quiz.q: Name two crevices that trap unburnt mixture in a petrol engine.
quiz.a: The top land gap above the top piston ring, the ring grooves, and the spark-plug thread.

quiz.q: Why does retarding the spark lower HC as well as NOx?
quiz.a: Retard lowers the peak burned-gas temperature, so less NO forms. It also makes the gas leave hotter, so more of the HC released from crevices and the oil film burns during expansion and in the exhaust port.

quiz.q: Why does NO peak slightly lean of stoichiometric instead of in the hottest rich mixture?
quiz.a: Thermal NO needs oxygen atoms as well as temperature. Near φ = 0.9 the burned gas is still very hot and spare oxygen is present. Richer mixtures have no spare oxygen; leaner ones run cooler.

quiz.q: Dry exhaust flow is 0.02 m³/s at standard conditions, CO reads 0.8 % and the brake power is 30 kW. Find the brake-specific CO (density of CO 1.25 kg/m³).
An exhaust stream of 6.0 kmol/h carries 1500 ppm NO. Find the NOx mass flow as NO<sub>2</sub>.
A cold engine idles with a rich mixture and late spark to warm the catalyst. Predict the engine-out CO, HC and NOx and give the reason for each.
quiz.a: CO is high, because the rich mixture lacks oxygen. HC is high, because fuel wets the cold walls and crevice gas does not burn in a cold exhaust, although late spark helps by making the exhaust hotter. NOx is low, because the rich mixture and late spark both lower the peak temperature and leave no spare oxygen.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engine makers now model NO formation with detailed chemistry inside computational fluid dynamics codes, and calibrate cold starts with spark retard, secondary air and close-coupled catalysts so most of the cycle’s HC is burnt in the first minute. Particle and HC emissions from direct-injection petrol engines, where fuel can wet the piston, are an active topic. Search next for “extended Zeldovich mechanism”, “crevice hydrocarbons” and “cold-start emissions”.

figure.caption: A sketch of the standard trends. CO and HC are high on the rich side and fall as the mixture leans out; NO peaks near φ = 0.9 (air–fuel ratio 16.3), the worked example’s mixture, and HC climbs again when a very lean charge misfires. The shaded band near 14.7 is where a three-way catalyst converts all three gases.

spec.aria: Engine-out CO, HC and NO against air-fuel ratio from 10 to 20. CO falls steeply from the rich side, HC falls and rises again beyond 18 where misfire starts, NO peaks at 16.3, which is equivalence ratio 0.9. A narrow band at 14.7 marks the catalyst window.
